Detect communities in networks

Source: R/add_clusters.R
add_clusters.Rd

The second step of the pipeline. In a bibliographic coupling network, groups of articles that cite the same literature, much more among themselves than with the rest of the network, are a usual operational definition of a research specialty or a research front (Boyack and Klavans 2010; Morris and Van der Veer Martens 2008) . add_clusters() finds such groups (communities, or clusters) with one of five algorithms of igraph, adds the cluster of each node and of each edge, and the relative size of each cluster. It works on one tbl_graph or on each graph of a list, as produced by build_dynamic_networks().

Most methods search for the partition that maximises the modularity (Newman and Girvan 2004) : the share of the edge weight that falls within clusters, minus the share expected if edges were placed at random given the weighted degree \(k_i\) of each node, $$Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \left( A_{ij} - \gamma \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right) \delta(c_i, c_j),$$ with \(A_{ij}\) the weight of the edge between \(i\) and \(j\), \(m\) the total weight, \(c_i\) the cluster of \(i\), and \(\gamma\) the resolution (1 in the original definition).

Usage

add_clusters(
  graphs,
  weights = NULL,
  clustering_method = c("leiden", "louvain", "fast_greedy", "infomap", "walktrap"),
  objective_function = c("modularity", "CPM"),
  resolution = 1,
  n_iterations = -1,
  n_groups = NULL,
  node_weights = NULL,
  trials = 10,
  steps = 4,
  verbose = TRUE,
  seed = NA
)

Arguments

graphs

A tbl_graph or a list of tbl_graphs.

weights

Edge weights. NULL (default) uses the weight edge column when it exists, NA ignores it, and a numeric vector gives the weights directly. Weights are read as strengths of ties: a larger weight pulls two nodes into the same cluster.

clustering_method

The algorithm, to choose explicitly among "leiden", "louvain", "fast_greedy", "infomap" and "walktrap" (see the details).

objective_function

For Leiden, the quality function to maximise: "modularity" or "CPM" (constant Potts model). Required for Leiden.

resolution

For Leiden, the resolution \(\gamma\). Higher values give more and smaller clusters.

n_iterations

For Leiden, the number of iterations of the algorithm. The default, -1, iterates until the partition no longer improves (see igraph::cluster_leiden()). A fixed number is much slower on large networks for no gain: on a window of 8,700 articles and 116,000 edges, 1,000 iterations took 44 s, against 0.6 s for -1, for the same modularity.

n_groups

For fast greedy and walktrap, an optional number of clusters at which to cut the dendrogram.

node_weights

For Leiden and Infomap, optional name of a node column with node weights (see igraph::cluster_leiden() and igraph::cluster_infomap()).

trials

For Infomap, the number of attempts to partition the network.

steps

For walktrap, the length of the random walks.

verbose

Logical. If TRUE (default), reports the number of clusters and the size of the largest one.

seed

Optional integer. Leiden, Louvain and Infomap are stochastic: two runs can give different partitions. A seed makes the result reproducible. It is set locally (with withr::local_seed()): the random-number stream of the session is left unchanged.

Value

The same object as graphs (a tbl_graph or a list of tbl_graphs) with the cluster columns described in the details, with the node table active.

Details

The algorithms.

  • "leiden" (Traag et al. 2019) , the default choice of recent bibliometric studies, improves on Louvain: it guarantees that clusters are connected, and iterating it refines the partition. It can maximise the modularity or the constant Potts model (CPM) (Traag et al. 2011) , which compares the internal weight \(e_c\) of each cluster with \(\gamma\) times its number of pairs, $$H = \sum_c \left( e_c - \gamma \binom{n_c}{2} \right):$$ a cluster is worth creating when its density exceeds \(\gamma\). Unlike the modularity, CPM does not depend on the size of the network, which makes clusters more comparable across networks of different sizes, but \(\gamma\) must then be set on the scale of the edge weights (with weights well below 1, resolution = 1 yields almost only singletons).

  • "louvain" (Blondel et al. 2008) , the greedy multi-level optimisation of modularity that Leiden refines.

  • "fast_greedy" (Clauset et al. 2004) , an agglomerative optimisation of modularity, deterministic.

  • "walktrap" (Pons and Latapy 2006) , which groups nodes that short random walks tend to visit together.

  • "infomap" (Rosvall and Bergstrom 2008) , which finds the partition that best compresses the description of a random walk on the network.

All algorithms are called from igraph (igraph::cluster_leiden(), igraph::cluster_louvain(), igraph::cluster_fast_greedy(), igraph::cluster_walktrap(), igraph::cluster_infomap()), and all use the edge weights unless weights = NA.

The resolution. Modularity has a resolution limit: in large networks, it can merge small but clear-cut communities (Fortunato 2010) . There is no single right number of clusters: a network of a discipline can be described at the level of fields or of specialties (Sjögårde and Ahlgren 2020) . Changing resolution, and checking that the main clusters persist across close values and across seeds (Traag et al. 2013) , is part of the analysis.

The output columns. With clustering_method = "leiden", nodes get cluster_leiden (identifiers numbered by decreasing cluster size, "01" being the largest, written with two digits so that they sort correctly) and size_cluster_leiden (the share of the nodes of the graph in the cluster). Edges get cluster_leiden_from, cluster_leiden_to and cluster_leiden, the latter being the common cluster of both ends, or "00" for edges between clusters. The edge cluster is what lets color_networks() give within-cluster edges the colour of their cluster. Other methods produce the same columns with their own suffix.

References

Blondel VD, Guillaume J, Lambiotte R, Lefebvre E (2008). “Fast Unfolding of Communities in Large Networks.” Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment, 2008(10), P10008. doi:10.1088/1742-5468/2008/10/P10008 .

Boyack KW, Klavans R (2010). “Co-Citation Analysis, Bibliographic Coupling, and Direct Citation: Which Citation Approach Represents the Research Front Most Accurately?” Journal of the American Society for Information Science and Technology, 61(12), 2389–2404. doi:10.1002/asi.21419 .

Clauset A, Newman MEJ, Moore C (2004). “Finding Community Structure in Very Large Networks.” Physical Review E, 70(6), 066111. doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.70.066111 .

Fortunato S (2010). “Community Detection in Graphs.” Physics Reports, 486(3), 75–174. doi:10.1016/j.physrep.2009.11.002 .

Morris SA, Van der Veer Martens B (2008). “Mapping Research Specialties.” Annual Review of Information Science and Technology, 42(1), 213–295. doi:10.1002/aris.2008.1440420113 .

Newman MEJ, Girvan M (2004). “Finding and Evaluating Community Structure in Networks.” Physical Review E, 69(2), 026113. doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.69.026113 .

Pons P, Latapy M (2006). “Computing Communities in Large Networks Using Random Walks.” Journal of Graph Algorithms and Applications, 10(2), 191–218. doi:10.7155/jgaa.00124 .

Rosvall M, Bergstrom CT (2008). “Maps of Random Walks on Complex Networks Reveal Community Structure.” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 105(4), 1118–1123. doi:10.1073/pnas.0706851105 .

Sjögårde P, Ahlgren P (2020). “Granularity of Algorithmically Constructed Publication-Level Classifications of Research Publications: Identification of Specialties.” Quantitative Science Studies, 1(1), 207–238. doi:10.1162/qss_a_00004 .

Traag VA, Krings G, Van Dooren P (2013). “Significant Scales in Community Structure.” Scientific Reports, 3, 2930. doi:10.1038/srep02930 .

Traag VA, Van Dooren P, Nesterov Y (2011). “Narrow Scope for Resolution-Limit-Free Community Detection.” Physical Review E, 84(1), 016114. doi:10.1103/PhysRevE.84.016114 .

Traag VA, Waltman L, van Eck NJ (2019). “From Louvain to Leiden: Guaranteeing Well-Connected Communities.” Scientific Reports, 9(1), 5233. doi:10.1038/s41598-019-41695-z .

See also

merge_dynamic_clusters() to follow clusters across time windows, name_clusters() to label them, add_node_roles() to characterise the position of nodes within and between clusters.

Examples

network <- build_network(
  nodes = subset(Nodes_stagflation, source_type == "Stagflation"),
  directed_edges = Ref_stagflation,
  source_id = "source_id",
  target_id = "target_id",
  projection_method = "structured",
  cooccurrence_method = "coupling_similarity",
  edges_threshold = 1
)

network <- add_clusters(
  network,
  clustering_method = "leiden",
  objective_function = "modularity",
  resolution = 1,
  seed = 123
)
#> ℹ "leiden" found 6 clusters; the largest gathers 36.1% of the nodes.
table(tidygraph::as_tibble(network, active = "nodes")$cluster_leiden)
#> 
#> 01 02 03 04 05 06 
#> 53 33 17 16 16 12
